title: Mass-access orbital transportation

concept.text: Mass-access orbital transportation is a complete, repeatable service that delivers useful cargo and, where appropriately qualified, people to orbit at a small fraction of comparable contemporary transportation costs. The target combines recovery of major flight hardware, rapid preparation for another flight, repeated reuse, and sustained safety and reliability. Its defining achievement would be dependable, affordable transportation across an operating fleet, rather than a successful recovery on an individual flight.

As a synthesis of the proposed concept, reuse matters only insofar as it improves the complete service. Recovering a stage preserves hardware, but the economic benefit also depends on how much inspection, repair, replacement, ground support and time are needed before it flies again, and how many useful flights it ultimately performs. Cost per delivered kilogram therefore needs to be assessed alongside payload capability, destination orbit, turnaround and reliability.

significance.text: The direct revolutionary consequence would be to relax the transportation-budget constraint on space activity. Conditional on delivering comparable service reliably at substantially lower fully accounted costs, projects could afford payloads or flight frequencies that their present transportation budgets exclude. This is a conditional economic inference; the supplied evidence does not quantify the resulting demand, establish affordability for particular customers or demonstrate mass access.

Large space industries, extensive infrastructure and settlements would be downstream possibilities, not automatic consequences. They would also require customers, destinations, energy, useful production processes and supporting systems. The supplied NASA inspector general review provides a concrete example of this interdependence: lunar landing development depends on concurrent progress in Orion, Gateway and next-generation spacesuits. Transportation can enable a broader activity without supplying everything that makes it viable.

A useful conceptual analogy is transportation infrastructure that enables many different activities by lowering the cost of reaching a destination. The analogy has limits: an orbital launch service would still operate within specified payload, orbit, safety and ground-infrastructure boundaries. Cheaper cargo delivery would not by itself establish inexpensive passenger travel, habitable destinations or economical transport beyond Earth orbit.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is integration of recovery, repeated reflight, rapid turnaround, low fully accounted costs and sustained reliability into one operational service. The supplied evidence establishes relevant progress and remaining challenges within particular programs, but does not establish that this complete capability was absent across the field on November 1, 2026. The concept remains a coherent target without a definitive field-wide absence claim.

As an engineering synthesis, major barriers include reentry protection that survives repeated flights, propulsion systems durable enough for repeated operation, and inspection methods that detect consequential damage without making refurbishment prohibitively slow or expensive. These elements interact: recovery can preserve a vehicle while leaving substantial repair work, and a vehicle that can fly again may still require too much labor or downtime to meet the intended service economics. The supplied audit does not directly establish repeated-reuse durability, propulsion-wear burdens or inspection requirements, so these are capability requirements rather than measured deficiencies attributed to a particular vehicle.

Ground operations and launch cadence must work alongside vehicle performance. At its evidentiary cutoff, the NASA audit reported that SpaceX had not demonstrated the 12- to 24-day launch-pad turnover required for the lunar mission architecture it examined. This is a concrete cadence challenge in that program. It is not a universal turnaround requirement for orbital transportation, nor does it by itself establish how long a recovered vehicle takes to prepare for reflight.

As an economic synthesis, the service must achieve enough useful flights per vehicle and enough demand to spread development, production, facilities and operating costs over delivered payloads. Faster turnaround creates potential capacity; it does not guarantee that customers will use that capacity. Safety assurance must also remain effective as flight rate rises, rather than depending on maintenance or inspection practices incompatible with the proposed cost and cadence.

current_state.text: According to the supplied validated review of NASA’s Management of the Human Landing System Contracts, dated March 10, 2026, Starship Flight 5 demonstrated a booster catch at the launch pad on October 13, 2024. The report also records that Flights 10 and 11 in 2025 each completed planned splashdowns of both the Starship vehicle and Super Heavy booster. These were completed splashdowns that occurred as planned, rather than announcements of future splashdown attempts.

The same report records New Glenn’s first-stage landing in November 2025. These results demonstrate specific recovery achievements. A catch, landing or splashdown does not by itself establish that the recovered hardware subsequently flew again, how much work reflight required, how many reuse cycles it could sustain or whether recovery reduced total transportation costs. The retained evidence therefore does not establish repeated operational reuse, rapid fleet turnaround or the economics of a fully reusable orbital service.

The earlier assertion that reusable first stages already operate through repeated reuse is not established by the supplied report’s recovery accounts. That evidentiary limitation does not show that the broader assertion is false; it means the retained source cannot substantiate it. Likewise, the report’s cost-control goals and cadence requirements are objectives and operational needs, not demonstrated low-cost service performance.

The evidence has both scope and access limitations. This is an audit of NASA’s lunar landing contracts, not a comprehensive assessment of orbital transportation. The supplied review verified the report’s identity and found the cited recovery passages readable, but worked from a partial extraction with PDF warnings, truncation on supplied Page 44 and no inspection of figures. The audit work extended through December 2025; its March 2026 publication date does not establish subsequent flight progress. With no supplied freshness record, developments through November 1, 2026 remain unassessed.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: multiple vehicles repeatedly deliver useful payloads to a specified orbit, recover and refly all major stages, and meet a turnaround limit declared before evaluation. Records should connect each delivered payload, recovery, maintenance interval and subsequent flight to the relevant hardware. This would test whether reuse and turnaround are repeatable properties of a fleet. The turnaround limit and required number of cycles remain to be selected; the supplied report establishes neither.
completion_criteria.label: Fleet repeatedly delivers payloads with major-stage reuse within declared turnaround

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic criterion: sustain an independently audited reduction of at least tenfold in fully accounted cost per delivered kilogram relative to comparable contemporary services. Define the payload, orbit, service requirements, accounting period, cost boundaries and utilization assumptions in advance. The comparison should distinguish customer price from the underlying cost of providing the service and make clear how development, hardware replacement, refurbishment, facilities and operations are treated. The tenfold threshold is a proposed ambition, not a demonstrated result or an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Audited full cost per delivered kilogram is tenfold below comparable services

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reliability criterion: specify the operational sample and required reliability threshold before assessment, then report successes, failures, maintenance and interruptions across that sample. Cargo delivery and passenger transport require separate statements of demonstrated capability; successful cargo operations alone would not establish suitability for people. A convincing record should cover repeated flights and maintenance cycles, rather than relying on a small set of selected successes.
completion_criteria.label: Reliability across repeated flights is reported against a predeclared threshold

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements: preserve records sufficient for independent reviewers to reproduce the turnaround, reliability and cost calculations, including uncertainty and sensitivity to utilization. Report the payload classes, orbit, fleet configuration, launch facilities and operating conditions over which the result was demonstrated. Finite trials establish performance within that tested breadth; they cannot establish universal affordability or reliability for every payload, destination or operating environment.
completion_criteria.label: Records enable independent reproduction of calculations within reported operating limits

related_concepts.text: Conceptual relationship to AER-02, A probe that returns data from another star system, and AER-08, A space observatory that can test for life on Earth-like exoplanets: cheaper orbital delivery could ease the launch and assembly constraints of ambitious scientific missions. Interstellar propulsion, long-distance communications and survival remain distinct requirements for AER-02, while the observing and measurement capabilities needed to test for life remain distinct requirements for AER-08. Orbital transportation alone would complete neither innovation.

Conceptual relationship to AER-03, Industrial production of spacecraft propellant from extraterrestrial resources, and AER-04, Multi-year, near-closed human life support for deep space: lower-cost launch could help deliver the equipment and supplies needed to develop either capability. AER-03 concerns producing propellant away from Earth, while AER-04 concerns sustaining people with limited resupply. Both could complement orbital transportation, but neither follows from recovering and reusing launch hardware.

Conceptual relationship to AER-05, Economically competitive space-to-Earth solar power, and AER-06, General-purpose robotic construction of very large space systems: affordable transport could reduce the cost of placing components, tools and replacement equipment in orbit. Solar power would still need competitive performance across generation, transmission and terrestrial delivery. Robotic construction would still need the ability to assemble and maintain large systems. These are complementary capabilities with separate completion tests.

Conceptual relationship to AER-07, An operational defense against civilization-threatening asteroid impacts: orbital transportation could support deployment of detection or intervention missions, but planetary defense also requires timely detection, characterization, effective intervention and operational coordination. Cheap launch alone does not establish an effective defense.

Conceptual relationship to AER-09, Sustained, useful air-breathing hypersonic flight, and AER-10, Fossil-fuel-free electric propulsion for large, long-range passenger aircraft: these entries overlap with orbital transportation in aerospace engineering, materials, thermal management, propulsion integration and safety assurance. Their operating regimes and intended services remain distinct. Air-breathing hypersonic flight does not itself demonstrate orbital delivery, and electric passenger-aircraft propulsion addresses atmospheric aviation rather than reusable access to orbit.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any service met the complete capability across the field on November 1, 2026, or what subsequent progress occurred.
Repeated operational first-stage reuse is asserted in the earlier material but is not substantiated by the retained recovery passages; no additional supporting source was supplied.
No supplied evidence establishes fleet-level fully accounted cost per kilogram, refurbishment burden, reuse lifetime or a tenfold cost reduction.
The proposed turnaround limit, required reuse cycles, operational sample and reliability threshold remain undefined.
Cost boundaries, comparable service requirements and utilization assumptions must be fixed before the proposed economic criterion can be evaluated.
The retained report extraction is partial, includes warnings and is truncated; figures were not inspected in the supplied review.
The supplied material does not quantify demand growth, customer affordability or the feasibility of downstream industries and settlements.

brief.title: Affordable, routine transport to orbit
possible: Space projects could send useful cargo to orbit more often, or send payloads their transport budgets cannot cover today. A fleet would recover its major rocket sections and fly them again with little delay, delivering dependable service at a fraction of current costs.
People could also travel on services qualified to carry them safely. The goal is an affordable, repeatable journey, with recovery and maintenance built into the service.
why: Transport costs constrain what space projects can attempt. Lower costs would let their budgets buy more delivered cargo or more frequent flights, opening room for activities that are currently too expensive.

sources.showed: The audit reported a Starship booster catch, planned splashdowns and a New Glenn first-stage landing. It also found schedule delays and technical challenges in lunar lander development.
sources.quote:
However, both SpaceX and  
Blue Origin have experienced schedule delays and face technical and integration challenges that have the potential to 
further impact lander costs and delivery schedules.
sources.cited_for: The audit documents rocket recovery achievements and operational challenges in lunar landing programs.
sources.not_established: Recovery alone does not establish repeated reuse, quick preparation for another flight or lower total transport costs.

sources.who: Katherine P. Van Hooser and Douglas P. Bradley
sources.showed: Reusable Space Shuttle main engines operated across 135 missions. Extensive testing and inspection between flights supported their performance.
sources.quote:
During the program over a million seconds of accumulated test and 
flight time was achieved.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates reusable engine operation and the role of testing and inspection in maintaining reliability.
sources.not_established: Engine performance alone does not establish a rapidly reusable fleet or affordable transport when all service costs are counted.

shown: SpaceX demonstrated a Starship booster catch and planned splashdowns of both rocket sections. Blue Origin landed New Glenn’s first stage. These achievements show that major hardware can return after flight.

NASA and Pratt & Whitney Rocketdyne’s Space Shuttle main engines operated across 135 missions. Their record shows that reusable engines can sustain flight operations with extensive testing and inspection.
missing: A fleet would need to combine repeated cargo delivery, recovery of all major stages and quick preparation for another flight.
Total costs would need to include development, repairs, replacement hardware, facilities and operations while remaining far below comparable services.
Reliability would need to hold across repeated flights and maintenance cycles, with passenger safety demonstrated separately.

milestones.label: Repeated fleet deliveries with timely reuse
milestones.explanation: Multiple vehicles would have to deliver useful cargo to a specified orbit and refly all major rocket sections within a declared time limit. This would establish repeatable reuse across a fleet.

milestones.label: Audited transport costs fall tenfold
milestones.explanation: An independent audit would have to show sustained total costs per delivered kilogram at least tenfold below comparable services. This would establish the economic benefit after all service costs are counted.

milestones.label: Repeated flights meet a declared reliability threshold
milestones.explanation: Flights and maintenance cycles would have to meet a reliability threshold set before assessment, with failures and interruptions reported. This would establish dependable service, with passenger capability assessed separately.

milestones.label: Independent reviewers reproduce the performance calculations
milestones.explanation: Independent reviewers would have to reproduce cost, reliability and time-between-flights calculations from operating records. This would establish performance within the tested payloads, orbits and operating conditions.

uncertain: The required time between flights, number of reuse cycles and reliability threshold remain undefined.
Cost comparisons depend on which services are comparable, which expenses count and how much customers use the fleet.
How much cheaper transport would expand demand, or support larger space industries and settlements, remains uncertain.

page.title: Reusable cargo transportation to low Earth orbit
page.definition: A launch service flies the same hardware on multiple missions to deliver bulk cargo to low Earth orbit, below about 2,000 km altitude. NASA’s space-solar-power benchmark specifies how much payload the service delivers in a year and what the customer pays per kilogram. Onward transport to the satellites’ operating orbit is priced separately.

goal.need: Deploying three Suntower solar power satellites a year would require roughly six times the payload mass launched worldwide in 2025. In two later space solar power designs, launch accounted for 71% and 77% of estimated total cost. Flying hardware again saves the cost of replacing it on every mission. Cheaper launch would bring electricity from orbit closer to the Suntower goal of five US cents per kilowatt-hour for terrestrial grids. Its price would still depend on the cost of moving the satellites from low Earth orbit to their operating orbit.

completion.criterion: A reusable launch service delivers more than 15,000 metric tons of payload to low Earth orbit in one year at a customer purchase price no greater than $400 per kilogram of payload, expressed in 1999 US dollars.
completion.set_by: NASA Space Solar Power study, Earth-to-orbit requirements and economic model in IAF-99-R.3.02, abstract and Tables 1.0 and 4.0.
completion.threshold_quote: over 15,000 metric tons to orbit per year at prices to the SSP system developer of only $400/kg

The study gives no operational acceptance protocol.

milestones.title: A reusable rocket engine is ground-tested for twice its permitted cumulative flight duration.
milestones.criterion: Ground hot-fire testing establishes a tested duration for the reusable engine design of at least twice its permitted cumulative flight duration.
milestones.set_by: NASA Space Shuttle Main Engine programme, flight-life qualification rule documented by NASA and Pratt & Whitney Rocketdyne; this threshold was written for Shuttle engines.
milestones.threshold_quote: every design was allowed to fly only 50% as long as it had been tested

milestones.title: An orbital-class launcher’s first stage completes a controlled landing or catch.
milestones.criterion: After separation from an orbital-class launcher, the first stage returns under control and either lands on a recovery surface or is caught by a launch tower.
milestones.set_by: SpaceX, SES-10 first-stage landing objective and Super Heavy tower-recovery design.
milestones.threshold_quote: Falcon 9’s first stage will attempt a landing

milestones.title: A recovered first stage flies again on a mission that delivers an orbital payload.
milestones.criterion: A first stage recovered from an earlier flight launches again on a mission that successfully delivers a payload to orbit.
milestones.set_by: SpaceX, SES-10 mission overview, published first-stage reflight objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: first reflight of an orbital class rocket.

milestones.title: An orbital launcher’s upper stage is recovered and reflown after booster reuse.
milestones.criterion: Recover and refly the upper stage of a two-stage orbital launcher whose booster has already been reused. SpaceX’s published Starship demonstration gate specifically requires a tower catch and reflight of the ship. Materials published on 4 June 2026 reported booster reuse and identified the ship’s catch and reflight as the remaining technical milestone. This developer report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: SpaceX Starship development programme, roadshow presentation published on 4 June 2026 and filed with the SEC, slide 21; the catch requirement was written for Starship’s tower-recovery architecture.
milestones.threshold_quote: the remaining technical milestone is the catch and re-flight of the ship

milestones.title: A reusable launch fleet delivers more than 15,000 metric tons of payload to low Earth orbit in one year.
milestones.criterion: The payload mass a reusable fleet delivers to low Earth orbit in one year exceeds 15,000 metric tons. This milestone measures delivered mass independently of customer price.
milestones.set_by: NASA Space Solar Power study, annual Earth-to-orbit transportation requirement in IAF-99-R.3.02.
milestones.threshold_quote: over 15,000 metric tons to orbit per year

milestones.title: One reusable booster completes ten flights in ten net calendar days.
milestones.criterion: The same booster completes ten flights within ten calendar days after subtracting range, weather and emergency delays. Range delays count as exclusions when the vehicle is fully flight-ready. The XS-1 campaign flies without an upper stage or payload and should represent the operational flight envelope in altitude, dynamic pressure and Mach number.
milestones.set_by: DARPA Experimental Spaceplane (XS-1) programme, 2016 programme overview, slides 3, 4 and 23.
milestones.threshold_quote: after subtracting range, weather, and emergency delays, 10 flights have taken place within a net period of 10 calendar days.

milestones.title: A launch tower catches the Starship upper stage returning from orbit.
milestones.criterion: The Starship upper stage returns from orbit and the launch tower’s mechanical arms catch it.
milestones.set_by: SpaceX Starship programme, upper-stage recovery design in the 2026 prospectus.
milestones.threshold_quote: caught mid-air by the launch tower’s mechanical arms.

milestones.title: A Starship upper stage caught by the launch tower flies again.
milestones.criterion: The same Starship upper stage that the launch tower caught after flight launches on a subsequent flight.
milestones.set_by: SpaceX Starship programme, upper-stage reflight objective in the June 2026 roadshow presentation, slide 21.
milestones.threshold_quote: the remaining technical milestone is the catch and re-flight of the ship

results.detail: Flight 5 took place on October 13, 2024. New Glenn demonstrated the recovery-surface alternative in November 2025.
results.quote:

using the launch tower arms.
